The Indian summer monsoon (ISM) is a major component of the Asian monsoon system, and exerts a critical influence on regional climate variability.
In this study, we reconstruct ISM variability from 184 − 25 ka using geochemical and environmental magnetic proxies from a lacustrine sediment core in the Heqing Basin, Southwest China.

In this study, we reconstruct ISM variability from 184 − 25 ka using geochemical and environmental magnetic proxies from a lacustrine sediment core in the Heqing Basin, Southwest China.

The proxy records reveal a pronounced dry-wet cycle throughout 184 − 25 ka: Phase I (184 − 131 ka) featured relatively weak ISM intensity and drier conditions; Phase II (131 − 69 ka) saw an overall increase in ISM intensity accompanied by higher rainfall; Phase III (69 − 57 ka) reverted to arid conditions; Phase IV (57 − 25 ka) exhibited a generally wetter climate, though punctuated by frequent major drought events.

Lacustrine sediments are highly sensitive to rapid climatic shifts and preserve detailed records of past climate events.
Researchers have used lacustrine sediments to investigate vegetation dynamics, monsoon mechanisms, lake level fluctuations, and erosion patterns 3 – 6 .
Southwestern China lies within a unique transition zone between the Indian and East Asian monsoon domains, and the regional climate responds directly to variations in the Indian Summer Monsoon (ISM).
Tectonic basins in this area contain thick, continuous lacustrine sequences that record environmental evolution over extended periods.
These lacustrine sediments are important archives for reconstructing ISM variability and local environmental history 7 – 9 .
These lacustrine sediments are important archives for reconstructing ISM variability and local environmental history 7 – 9 .
However, the driving mechanisms of ISM variability from millennial to orbital timescales remain debated 10 , 11 .
However, the driving mechanisms of ISM variability from millennial to orbital timescales remain debated 10 , 11 .

For example, on millennial timescales, some studies suggest that ISM variability was paced by Northern Hemisphere summer insolation (NHSI) 12 , whereas others emphasize the influence of Southern Hemisphere temperatures 13 .

Researchers have employed a variety of proxies to investigate ISM variability, including carbon and oxygen isotopes 15 , 16 , physical parameters 13 , 17 , biological markers 8 , 18 , and geochemical proxies 19 , 20 .
Different proxies often exhibit varying sensitivities to monsoon variability 21 , 22 , and interpretations of the same proxy may differ among regions 23 .
Here, we present a high-resolution paleoclimate study of the Heqing Basin based on major geochemical compositions and environmental magnetic proxies spanning 184 − 25 ka.
We further examine ISM variability on both glacial-interglacial and millennial timescales, and discuss the likely driving mechanisms.
Sampling and material The Heqing Basin is a tectonic fault basin surrounded by high mountains.
It receives ~ 900–1000 mm of annual precipitation, ~ 80–90% of which falls in summer.
The PT2 drill core is 33.9 m long and consists primarily of grayish-green clay and silt.

Discussion Environmental evolution in the Heqing basin from 184 to 25 ka Based on the integrated responses of magnetic and non-magnetic proxies, we divide the 184 − 25 ka interval into four phases (I-IV) from bottom to top (Fig.
In Phase I (184 − 131 ka; approximately MIS 6), the lithology is relatively uniform and dominated by grayish-green clay.
Higher Ti values suggest enhanced physical erosion in the catchment and more detrital influx 41 .
The χ-T curves show an obvious maghemite component, implying comparatively weak reductive dissolution during this interval.
The evidence above indicates ISM weakening and reduced rainfall during this interval.
Reduced concentration-dependent magnetic parameters (χ, ARM, SIRM), lower Rb/Sr ratios, and higher CaCO₃ contents collectively indicate a more humid climate and a stronger ISM.

In Phase III (69 − 57 ka; approximately MIS 4), the lithology is dominated by grayish-green clay.
This pattern indicates drier conditions when ISM weakened, subsequently increase physical erosion, and more detrital influx into the lakes.
